segments.narration: Four kilometres under Antarctic ice, a lake never froze. Vostok runs 250 kilometres long, fifty wide, and up to 900 metres deep.
Its water sits near minus three degrees and stays liquid anyway, squeezed by hundreds of bars of pressure from the ice overhead.
It has been sealed off from the sky for roughly fifteen million years. So what has been living down there all that time?
Russian drillers reached the water in February 2012, nearly 3,770 metres down, through a borehole held open with kerosene and Freon.
That was the problem. By May 2017 the Russian team reported their water samples were too contaminated to say anything reliable about the lake.

verdicts.claim: Lake Vostok lies about 4,000 m beneath the ice surface in East Antarctica, is 250 km long and 50 km wide, with a maximum depth reported between 510 and 900 m.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia gives about 4,000 m below the ice surface, 250 km by 50 km, and a maximum depth of 510 to 900 m depending on the source; Phys.org describes it as beneath nearly 4 km of ice.

verdicts.claim: Lake Vostok's average water temperature is about -3 degrees Celsius and it stays liquid because of the pressure of the overlying ice, reported at roughly 345 to 355 bars.

verdicts.claim: Lake Vostok's water is estimated to have been sealed under the ice for about 15 million years.

verdicts.claim: Russian drilling reached the lake's water surface in February 2012, at roughly 3,770 m depth, through a borehole kept open with about 60 short tons of Freon and kerosene.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia gives February 2012 (5 February for the 3,768 m core, 6 February for water) and about 60 short tons of Freon and kerosene in the borehole; Talalay's figure for contact is 3,769.3 m, so the narration rounds to 'nearly 3,770 metres'.

verdicts.claim: In May 2017 Russian researchers reported their water samples were too contaminated to yield reliable data on the lake's chemistry or biology.
